opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of it comes down to optionality. When an investor is unsure, saying a clear "no" closes a door, and in venture, closing doors is expensive. If they pass explicitly and the company later becomes something big, that's a visible miss, and it can also damage the relationship. Founders remember who said no. So the rational move, from their side, is to keep the conversation warm: "Let's stay in touch," "Keep us posted on your progress," "We'd love to see a few more data points." None of those are rejections, but none of them are commitments either.

There's also the social dynamic. Most investors are genuinely nice people, and they don't want to be the one who crushes a founder's enthusiasm, especially early on when the founder is pouring everything into it. A soft non-answer feels kinder in the moment, even if it isn't actually kinder for the founder.

And honestly, part of it is information-gathering. If they don't say no, they get to watch. They see who else comes in, whether a lead investor emerges, how the team executes over the next few months. Then they can decide with much less uncertainty. A lot of investors are really following signals from other investors, so staying in a "maybe" state lets them wait for that signal.

For me as a founder, the lesson was learning to read "maybe" as "not yet, and probably not," and to not spend too much time hoping. I'd rather get a fast no than a slow maybe, because time is the most precious resource when you're building. So I've tried to ask more direct questions, like "What would you need to see to commit?" or "Is this a pass for now?" Sometimes people appreciate that directness, and it saves everyone a lot of energy.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: I think the honest answer is that a clear "no" costs an investor something, and a vague "let's keep in touch" costs them nothing. When they're unsure, saying no means closing a door. If we end up doing well, that no becomes a visible mistake, something they have to explain to their partners or that circulates in the ecosystem. But if they stay ambiguous, they preserve optionality. They can come back in six months when there's more signal, more revenue, a bigger name on the cap table, and the earlier hesitation is forgotten.

There's also a social dimension. Venture is a relationship business, and the founder you reject today might be the founder who introduces you to the next deal, or who raises a huge round elsewhere. So being direct feels risky in a way that being warm and noncommittal doesn't. Nobody wants to be the person who was rude to the company that later became important.

And frankly, a lot of the time they genuinely don't know. They're not lying when they say they need to think about it. The uncertainty is real. They're trying to pattern-match against things they've seen, and sometimes what you're doing doesn't fit any pattern yet. So instead of forming a judgment, they wait for someone else to form one first. That's why the first committed check matters so much more than its dollar amount. It converts "I'm not sure" into "someone I respect is sure."

What I learned is to treat the absence of a clear no as a no, operationally. Not emotionally, but in terms of how I allocate time. If someone isn't moving toward a term sheet, they are effectively passing, whatever the language. The founders who get burned are the ones who read politeness as momentum and keep spending weeks on a conversation that was already over.

r002.rationale: It describes preserving relationships and avoiding the risk of being rude to a future-successful founder, but does not say investors fear Carina will disregard them in the future.

astra-6.text: I think there’s an asymmetry in the incentives. If an investor says no, they risk closing the door on a company that might turn out to be successful. If they say, “Let’s stay in touch,” they preserve the option to invest later, once there’s more traction or someone else has committed. And there’s also the human side: rejecting someone directly can be uncomfortable. So uncertainty often comes across as encouragement, even when there isn’t a real intention to invest.

sol-6.1.text: I think investors have an incentive to keep their options open. If they say no explicitly, they risk closing the door. But if they say, “Let’s stay in touch,” they can wait to see whether you gain traction or other investors get interested. From the founder’s perspective, that can feel like encouragement, even when there isn’t much conviction behind it. So I’d treat anything short of a concrete next step as uncertainty, rather than a yes.
